title: Rate rise bets jump after RBA inflation warning
full_text:
Reserve Bank deputy governor Andrew Hauser says the central bank faces a hard decision on whether to raise interest rates for the fifth time this year, with inflation materially worse than the bank's expectations despite softening employment and consumption.
Hauser's final individual appearance before the RBA monetary policy board meets on November 2-3 put borrowers on notice that the cash rate could rise to its highest level since 2008. Traders now rate a fifth increase for the year to be more likely than not.
"The inflation outlook looks materially worse than we projected in the August report," Hauser told the Citi Investment Conference on Wednesday, even as the economy slowed elsewhere.
"[The] labour market is easing, consumption growth is quite tepid, but there are still pockets of growth and the inflation outlook has deteriorated. So that's a pretty tricky balance".
Inflation data for the September quarter will be released on October 28, which economists expect to show cost pressures continuing to run hot across the economy.
That could bolster the chances of a Melbourne Cup day rate rise, which markets had priced in at 27 per cent before Hauser began his remarks to 57 per cent afterwards. An increase to the borrowing cost is fully priced in by March and markets are betting on a small chance of a sixth.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers acknowledged the mounting problems for the Australian economy on Wednesday, and once again attributed these pressures to the Iran war. Hauser also cited the war as a factor, alongside the AI boom and domestic capacity pressures.
"From an economic point of view, the war in the Middle East has created a very difficult set of conditions for a lot of countries, including ours," Chalmers said in an interview with CNBC Australia. "You can see it in our inflation, which is a bit higher than we would like. We can see it in our growth. You can see it in other areas as well."
Hauser said the economic data to date had left the bank with "hard choices".
"The challenge that's facing the board and has done for some time is do you do more to tackle higher inflation, recognising that that means weaker activity, weaker labour market," he said. "Those are hard choices; they're not where we'd like to be ideally as the central bank."
Rising inflation expectations were an additional headache for the bank.
"We are beginning to see some signs that some people in the community are not sure if we're going to bring inflation back into target at all, or certainly not for an extended period," said Hauser, citing findings from Macquarie University that a growing proportion of businesses thought inflation above the 2 per cent to 3 per cent target was "normal".
"That is the central banker's nightmare," he said.
Central banks try to keep inflation expectations in check to prevent widespread anticipation of ever-increasing inflation triggering price spirals across the economy.
Betashares chief economist David Bassanese said the RBA was likely to respond swiftly to evidence that inflation expectations were rising.
"The RBA seems increasingly prepared to risk a recession to get inflation down," he said. "The economy is slowing, house prices are slumping, interest rates are restrictive, unemployment is going up, and they still want to do more."
Economists at Goldman Sachs updated their rate forecasts to include a rise next month following Hauser's "clearly hawkish" appearance.
"Today's remarks suggest the RBA continues to see risks to inflation and inflation expectations as tilted to the upside even with the delivered 100 basis point tightening year-to-date," said Andrew Boak, the bank's chief economist for Australia and New Zealand.
"In our view - absent a downside surprise in the CPI report due on 28 October - [those risks] make a further hike in November more likely than not."
Hauser's hawkishness came despite employment data released last week showing the unemployment rate had unexpectedly steadied at a five-year high of 4.7 per cent, more than a year in advance of when the RBA's own forecasts indicated it would hit that rate.
On Wednesday, Hauser said that while there were signs the labour market was easing, the unemployment rate was still low by historical and international standards.
"No lost job is one to celebrate. I would never say that, but these are still quite low numbers internationally and relative to history," he said, adding there was debate under way at the RBA about their refreshed unemployment forecasts set for release next month.
RBA governor Michele Bullock suggested last month that a 5 per cent unemployment rate was the top of the range needed to rein in inflation.
"Whether it goes to 5 [per cent], whether it goes to some other number, that's a debate we're having in the context of our forecast at the moment. And you'll see our answers to that in a week or two," Hauser said, which market economists interpreted as an indication the RBA's unemployment forecast could rise beyond 5 per cent.
